newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee breaks above $1,700 in pursuit of NY.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee breaks above $1,700 in pursuit of NY.

text.p: Robusta coffee futures, carried by New York's relentless momentum, set its third gap on Thursday, breaking above $1,700 to score a six-month high.

Traders were getting increasingly dubious about a continued rally, which has now extended total gains to 42 percent since early January, but no-one was prepared to sell while the market bubbled at a new technical high ground.
"Who wants to jump in front of a runaway train", said one, adding that some traders were caught short on Thursday and got their fingers burnt.
"We've come such a long way without any real consolidation that everybody's expecting it. But for the time being the market has a momentum of its own," said another.
The morning's 3,758 lots turnover saw a mixed bunch of trade buying and selling as they juggled positions. Roasters were also buying but "by now some of them are sitting on a decent cover," said one.
The May contract, in its pursuit of sharp gains in New York on Wednesday, opened $51 higher, but snubbed a call for $60 higher. It ended at a midsession level of $1,705 a tonne, up $38 on the day.

The CSCE Arabica coffees soared for the fifth straight day on Wednesday as hedge buying by roasters and fund speculation extended the four-week-old rally. March gained 8.30 cents to 171.85 cents a lb after reaching a new contract high of 173 cents.
Technically, London seemed well supported below $1,600 and seemed pushing higher towards $1,740, but analysts cautioned of a possible assault to $1,550.

"If we are going to see a failure at the highs, we're going to have to move back aggressively into that range beneath $1,640, probably well back, I should think below $1,550," said Susan Rigg of Chart Analysis.
Traders said Monday's President's Day in United States could be used as an opportunity to take profits on Friday before the long weekend.
And a close below $1,590 and $1,540 on May could begin to shake speculative funds out of London.

Former USDA analyst Leon Yallouz denied talk that he forecast Brazil's 1997/98 crop at 24 million or 27 million bags. "There is no truth in that," he told Reuters in Sao Paolo but did not say what his estimate was.
In Colombia, where a major state-sector strike has crippled road transport, talks between union leaders and government ministers were due to restart at 7 a.m. Thursday (1200 GMT).
But there were doubts whether the two sides would be able TO shake hands quickly to end the country's biggest labour unrest in 20 years.
